overview: This map category spans many Amazonian societies, not a single civilization. Evidence from particular places shows hunting, fishing, gathering, cultivation and settlement in different combinations. The examples below describe those places; none defines everyone within the map’s broad outline.

periods.title: Early cultivation in southwestern Amazonia
periods.summary: At forest-island sites in the Llanos de Moxos, plant microfossils document early manioc and squash cultivation, followed later by maize. These local developments overlapped with long histories of foraging.

periods.title: Earthwork construction in Acre
periods.summary: The 2018 regional comparison places an early flourishing of Acre’s geometric earthworks in these centuries. Their history differs from the later peak of enclosure construction farther east and south.

periods.title: Villages and earthworks in parts of southern Amazonia
periods.summary: Ditched settlements expanded in parts of southern Amazonia. Pottery styles and settlement arrangements differ between regions, so shared earth-building practices do not demonstrate one Amazon-wide state.

periods.title: Colonial disruption in the Upper Xingu
periods.summary: Kuikuro historical accounts describe slave-raiding encounters and later epidemic losses. Communities moved and regrouped while maintaining identities and relationships. This is an Upper Xingu sequence, not a single chronology for all Amazonia.

items.text: At Caverna da Pedra Pintada near Monte Alegre, excavators found triangular stone spear points, other tools and paintings in a stratified cave site. Radiocarbon dates on charred plant remains and luminescence measurements support a late Pleistocene occupation. The evidence documents people living in a tropical environment long before the map’s first appearance of this category.

Charred tree fruits, wood and animal remains at Pedra Pintada indicate a varied forest-and-river economy. The inhabitants cannot be described only as big-game hunters. Their food debris gives evidence of gathering and using local environments, although surviving remains are not a complete menu of everything eaten.

At Isla del Tesoro in Bolivia’s Llanos de Moxos, layers of burnt and unburnt apple-snail shells occur with other animal remains. Broken deer bone, localized burning, sediment chemistry and stratigraphy together support human food preparation. A shell accumulation by itself would not establish that people, rather than animals or natural processes, made the mound.

The Isla del Tesoro study interprets repeated burnt lenses as intermittent, possibly seasonal use. Snails may have supplemented other foods despite dominating the preserved deposit. As refuse accumulated, the mound became a raised place within wetland surroundings. This is evidence of changing a landscape through repeated activity, without requiring a planned monumental construction.

At Llanos de Moxos forest islands, microscopic silica traces left by plants identify manioc, squash and maize. The 2020 study reports manioc at about 10,350 calibrated years before present and maize later, around 6,850. These are dated local attestations, not proof that one crop appeared everywhere at once or that gathering immediately ended.

At Hatahara in central Amazonia, dark soil contains fragmented charcoal, bone and pottery. At nearby Caldeirão, excavations reveal mounds and pits, including a pit with well-preserved vessels. These archaeological contexts support a strong human role in forming fertile soils, rather than treating every dark patch as a natural river deposit.

The 2023 dark-earth study compared modern Indigenous settlements with archaeological sites in the Upper Xingu. Similarities in soil composition and distribution, together with documented soil-enriching practices, support deliberate management as one explanation for ancient fertile patches. The comparison is a model grounded in evidence, not direct access to every ancient household’s intentions.

Researchers at Kuikuro II observed people spreading hearth ash, charcoal and manioc-processing waste, and planting crops in enriched ground near houses. Farmers explained the intended improvement of the soil in interviews. These observations connect everyday cooking, cleaning and food preparation with cultivation, while leaving room for variation between households and statements.

Excavation at the Upper Tapajós site Mt-04 found pottery and charcoal within dark earth inside a ditched enclosure. Charcoal associated with pottery near the deposit’s base dated to 1410 to 1460 CE. The dense domestic remains support settlement use; the ditch alone would not establish how the place functioned.

Mt-04 pottery differs in decoration from ceramics reported in Acre, Bolivia and the Upper Xingu. Communities could share the practice of constructing earthworks while retaining different craft traditions. That variation matters when interpreting a map that gives large areas a single label.

Dark-earth chemistry does not translate directly into a population count. The 2022 assessment explains that people concentrated food residues and other materials from a wider catchment into settlement areas. Understanding ordinary refuse disposal is therefore essential before using enriched soil to infer farming intensity or the size of a community.

Kuikuro oral history recounts slave-raiding encounters before peaceful exchanges with Karl von den Steinen in the nineteenth century. Later influenza and measles caused severe losses and movements closer to medical posts. This documented community history shows why village abandonment and population decline must be distinguished from the disappearance of Indigenous peoples.

ending.text: This regional category has no single founding, conqueror or fall. Individual societies followed different paths through colonial violence, disease, migration and continuing community life. Kuikuro history provides one example of that continuity. The map’s 1800 cutoff does not mark the extinction of Amazonian peoples or the end of foraging.
